Introduction:
Endometrial (EC), epithelial ovarian (EOC), and cervical cancers (CC) are among the most common cancers in females, and substantial causes of cancer-related mortality [ 1 ].

Statins, widely used to treat and prevent cardiovascular diseases, inhibit 3-hydroxy-3-methylglutaryl-coenzyme A (HMGCoA) reductase, leading to reduced cholesterol levels and inhibition of proteins involved in the development and progression of several cancers, including gynecological cancers [ 2 , 3 ]. Previous studies on statin use and gynecological cancer risk have reported conflicting results [ 3 , 4 ]. These studies have often been impaired by small sample size and limited data on associations by type of statin (e.g. lipophilic, hydrophilic) and in disease subgroups (e.g. histological subtypes).

We used a large population-based cohort (>1 million women) to assess the association between use of statins and the risk of EC, EOC, and CC, including stratified analyses by type of statin, strength of statin, age, histology, and body mass index (BMI).
Methods:
### Study design, population, and data sources

We used the Population Registry from Statistics Norway [ 5 ] to identify women born between 1925 and 1986 who lived in Norway at any time in 2004–18, forming the underlying cohort. Women entered the analytic cohort for the current study on the latest of: 1 January 2004, the date they turned 49.5 years old, or their first immigration date. Women born in 1968 or later did not turn 50 before end of follow-up, and therefore could not enter the analytic cohort. Follow-up started 6 months after cohort entry to ensure 6 months of medication history. Statin use is uncommon among women <50 years in Norway, thus we included only women aged ≥50 years at the start of follow-up. We excluded women with a history of invasive cancer prior to the start of follow-up {except invasive non-melanoma skin cancer [International Classification of Diseases (ICD) version 10 code: C44]}. Women were followed until they were diagnosed with EC, EOC, or CC (the outcomes of interest in the separate analyses), diagnosed with a different invasive cancer, died, emigrated, or on 31 December 2018, whichever occurred first.

Medication data were obtained from the Norwegian Prescription Database, which have detailed information on all dispensed prescriptions from community pharmacies since January 2004 [ 6 ] including: date, Anatomical Therapeutic Chemical (ATC) code, amount (number of tablets), strength (e.g. mg per tablet), and number of defined daily doses (DDD). One DDD is the average dose associated with one day of use if the medication is prescribed for its main indication to an adult [ 7 ]. Data on cancer diagnoses were obtained from the Cancer Registry of Norway [ 8 ]. Date of birth, migration, educational level, income, marital status, country of origin/birth, and the number of children were obtained from Statistics Norway [ 9 ]. Date of death was obtained from the Cause of Death Registry [ 10 ]. BMI was available for a subset of women who participated in selected health surveys, as described previously [ 11 ]. We used the BMI measurement closest to the start of follow-up, with a maximum of 5 years before or after the start of follow-up (92% of the measurements are pre-diagnostic).

### Consent to participate

Informed consent is not needed for use of registry data. Informed consent for the health surveys was collected by the team collecting the data for the health surveys.

### Exposure assessment

Statin use (ATC code: C10AA, C10BA02, C10BA05 as these are marketed in Norway) was based on dispensed prescriptions. Treatment days were calculated using the number of DDDs, assuming one DDD per day. To account for use beyond the estimated treatment days (i.e. use <1 DDD per day), we added a 4-month grace period to the initially estimated duration of statin use. We analyzed the exposure to statins as a time-dependent variable. Women contributed person-time as never, current, or past users. Women with no statin dispensation during the 6 months before start of follow-up contributed time as never users from the start of follow-up until the date of the first dispensed statin prescription ( Supplementary Fig. S1 ). Women contributed person-time as current users from the date of dispensation until the end of the estimated duration of statin use. In cases where there were gaps between the end of the estimated duration of use and the next dispensation of statin, women contributed person-time as past users from the end of the estimated duration until the next dispensation of statin or end of follow-up. Women with a period of current use that covered the start of follow-up began contributing person-time as current users from the start of follow-up. Women who were dispensed a prescription of statin in the 6 months before the start of follow-up, with an estimated duration not covering the start of follow-up, contributed person-time as past users from the start of follow-up. Women who were dispensed a statin between cohort entry and start of follow-up were defined as prevalent users, while women who were dispensed their first statin after start of follow-up were defined as incident users. To limit reverse causation, we applied a 6-month lag-time period to all prescriptions [ 12 ].

Statin use was assessed overall and by type (lipophilic and hydrophilic; Supplementary Table S1 ) and strength (low, medium, high [ 13 ]). Women could be users of different types and strengths of statins (i.e. they are not censored for the previous type or strength when starting a new type or strength of statin, and the statistical models are mutually adjusted for the different types and strengths of statins).

### Outcome assessment

The outcomes were diagnoses of EC (ICD-10: C54), EOC (including fallopian tube and primary peritoneal cancers) (C48.2, C56, C57.0–C57.4), or CC (C53). Non-carcinomatous cancers, such as sarcomas, lymphomas, and neuroendocrine tumors were excluded. Histologic subgroups were categorized using morphology codes ( Supplementary Table S2 ).

### Nested-case control study

In addition to the cohort design, we conducted a nested-case control study to evaluate duration of statin use and time since cessation and risk of EC, EOC, and CC. To accurately estimate the cumulative DDDs and time since cessation in the nested-case control study, we excluded prevalent statin users (see “Exposure assessment”) at baseline from the original cohort. Each case was matched with 10 controls who were at risk of an incident cancer diagnosis at the age and date when the corresponding case was diagnosed (index date). We defined the exposure based on status at the index date ( Supplementary Fig. S2 ) and created a variable with 7 categories: never use, 3 levels of time since cessation (<1, 1–2.9, and ≥3 years since last period of current use), and 3 levels of current use (based on cumulative DDD; <548 DDDs, 548–1824, and ≥1825 DDDs).

### Statistical analysis

Cox proportional hazard models were used to estimate hazard ratios (HRs) with 95% confidence intervals (CIs) in the cohort design. Age was the underlying time scale. Conditional logistic regression models were used to estimate associations in the nested-cased control study. Estimates were adjusted for a priori selected covariates registered at cohort entry in the cohort design and at index date in the nested-case control design: age in years (underlying time scale in the cohort design and matching variable in the nested-case control design), education (none/primary school only, secondary school, higher education, missing), income (quartiles), marital status (married/partnered, not married/partnered, missing), country of origin/birth (Norway, other countries), number of children (0, 1, 2, ≥3). All estimates were also adjusted for use of other individual medications during follow-up (≥1 dispensed prescription of the specific medication), including beta-blockers (ATC code: C07), calcium channel blockers (C08), agents acting on the renin–angiotensin system (C09), diuretics (C03), low-dose aspirin (B01AC06, B01AC56), antidiabetics (A10), non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs (NSAIDs; M01A), and menopausal hormone therapy (G03C, G03F). The women were defined as never users until their first dispensed prescription of the specific medication, from that date onwards they were defined as ever users. Missing information on covariates was handled as a separate category in the variable.

We evaluated risk of EC, EOC, and CC overall, and in subgroups defined by type and strength of statin, age (attained age or age at index: 50–64.9 years, 65–94 years, in the cohort analysis the follow-up time was left truncated at the lower age interval and censored at the upper age interval for the two age categories), histology, and BMI (<25, ≥25 kg/m 2 ). The cutoff level for BMI was set as it represents the definition of overweight and can therefore give clinically relevant information using a readily available metric. We also performed an analysis in the subset of women with a BMI measurement adjusting for BMI as a continuous variable. Prevalent users, as described previously, were excluded from the cohort analysis in a sensitivity analysis.

All tests were two-sided with a 5% significance level. Statistical analyses were performed using R software version 4.2.3 ( http://cran.r-project.org/ ).
Results:
We identified 1 872 600 women who resided in Norway at any point between 2004 and 2018. After excluding women who lived in Norway <6 months ( n = 15 311), those with a history of cancer ( n = 64 064), and those not reaching age 50 by the end of 2018 ( n = 709 596), 1 083 629 women were included. During median follow-up of 11.6 years, 334 582 (31%) women used statins at least once (90% did not switch between hydrophilic and lipophilic statins), and 7709 EC cases, 4415 EOC cases, and 1603 CC cases were identified. At the start of follow-up, women who used statins at least once were generally older, and more likely to have only mandatory education, low income, be born in Norway, have children, and use other medications compared to women who had never used statins ( Table 1 ). BMI was available for 450 143 (42%) women; among those, a higher proportion of women with BMI ≥ 25 was found among statin users (60.7%), as compared to non-users (47.3%). The cumulative time as a user of statins during the study period was longer among the women categorized as current users at the end of follow-up (median = 7.12 years, Quartile 1 = 3.05 and Quartile 3 = 11.50) as compared to those categorized as past users (median = 2.96 years, Quartile 1 = 1.02 and Quartile 3 = 6.95).

Inverse associations were observed between statin use, compared to no use, and EC risk [current: HR = 0.90 (95% CI: 0.85–0.96), past: HR = 0.79 (0.71–0.88)] ( Fig. 1 ). Associations were similar in analyses stratified by age and histology. In analyses by statin type, associations were observed for lipophilic [e.g. current: HR = 0.90 (0.85–0.96)] but not hydrophilic statins [current: HR = 1.09 (0.92–1.29)]. No consistent pattern was observed by strength. When considering the subset of women with BMI data, the estimate for the association between statin use and EC risk was similar to that observed in the full cohort [current: HR = 0.90 (0.82–0.99); past: HR = 0.85 (0.72–1.00)], and was not impacted by adjustment for BMI [current: HR = 0.90 (0.82–0.99); past: HR = 0.84 (0.71–1.00)].

No significant association was observed between statin use and EOC risk overall [current: HR = 1.07 (0.99–1.16); past: HR = 1.04 (0.91–1.19)] ( Fig. 2 ). The estimates were consistent across different subgroups defined by type and strength of statin, age, and histology, with the exception of a significant inverse association observed between past use and risk of high-grade serous EOC [HR = 0.78 (0.62–0.99)].

Current statin use was not associated with CC risk [HR = 1.02 (0.89–1.18)], but past use was [HR = 0.71 (0.53–0.94)] ( Fig. 3 ). Overall, estimates in subgroups defined by type of statin, strength of the statin, age, and histology did not differ substantially, though significant inverse associations were observed with past use, but not current use, of medium-strength statins, and past use among women ages 50–64 years [e.g. medium-strength statins, current use: HR = 1.04 (0.89–1.22); past use: HR = 0.68 (0.53–0.88)].

When stratified by BMI (<25, ≥25 kg/m 2 ) the estimates for all three cancers were similar to those for the overall populations ( Supplementary Tables S3–S5 ). Findings were similar when restricting the cohort to only those categorized as non-users at baseline (i.e. excluding past and current users; data not shown).

Overall results for current and past use were similar in the cohort and nested-case control designs. In the nested-case control studies evaluating cumulative DDDs for current users and time since cessation among past users, we included 7642 women with EC and 76 420 controls ( Supplementary Tables S6 and S7 ), 4379 women with EOC and 43 790 controls ( Supplementary Tables S8 and S9 ), and 1576 women with CC and 15 760 controls ( Supplementary Tables S10 and S11 ). We found no trends in the association with cumulative DDDs or time since cessation for any cancer type in the overall population or in any of the subgroups ( Supplementary Tables S7, S9 , and S11 ).
Discussion:
In this large population-based cohort, statin use was associated with lower EC risk. These associations were observed only for lipophilic statins, and associations were similar across subgroups defined by age, histology, and BMI. We observed no trend in the association by cumulative DDDs or time since last use. We found limited evidence of associations between statin use and EOC or CC.

A proposed mechanism supporting the hypothesis that statins may reduce cancer risk involves their inhibition of HMGCoA-reductase, the rate-limiting enzyme in the mevalonate pathway. This inhibition lowers cholesterol levels and interferes with the synthesis of other proteins known to be implicated in carcinogenesis [ 2 , 3 ]. Additionally, statins might exert an anticancer effect through a mechanism independent of the mevalonate pathway by disrupting the interaction between integrin LFA-1 and intracellular adhesion molecule 1 (ICAM1) and thereby affecting the invasion, migration, and cell adhesion [ 2 ]. Specific to EC, statins may be associated with decreased risk via reductions in total cholesterol, and downstream reductions in estrogen receptor-modulating cholesterol metabolites such as 27-hydroxycholesterol [ 14 ], which has agonist activity in the normal corpus uteri [ 15 , 16 ], and has been linked to EC in experimental models [ 17 ].

Current statin use was associated with a 10% lower EC risk and past use with a 21% lower risk. These associations were consistent when adjusted for and stratified by BMI, and across age and histology subgroups. Our findings align with results from previous studies using data from population-based databases [ 18–20 ], as well as large prospective cohorts [ 21 , 22 ]. These studies reported risk reductions ranging from 22% to 85%. While we found an association for both short-term and long-term statin use, prior studies have reported a reduced EC risk only for longer-term use of statins [ 20 , 22 ]. Further, while we observed associations predominantly for lipophilic statins (the predominant type prescribed in our study), others evaluating associations for lipophilic and hydrophilic statins have found no difference in association by statin type [ 20 , 21 ]. Lipophilic statins have been shown to decrease endometrial stromal cell proliferation [ 23 ] and inversely impact inflammation-related pathways [ 24 ], while the investigated hydrophilic statins (pravastatin [ 23 ]; rosuvastatin [ 24 ]) did not induce these effects. Further studies, all evaluating ever vs. never statin use, have observed no associations with EC risk, which might be due to differences in population characteristics, and patterns of prescribing and use of statins [ 25–28 ].

We found limited evidence of an association between statins and EOC risk. This is consistent with most previous studies [ 21 , 25 , 26 , 28–30 ], though some studies have suggested a protective effect of statins against EOC [ 20 , 31 ]. The only significant associations observed in the current study were between past use of statins and high-grade serous EOC. Though these findings were not fully consistent, they align with the associations observed for EC, and notably for type II (primarily serous) EC, and with the potential common origins of a subset of high-grade serous EOC and EC in the fallopian tube [ 32 ]. While there are commonalities in risk factors for endometrioid EOC and EC [ 33 , 34 ], we observed a lack of agreement in the associations between statins and these subtypes, though the number of endometrioid EOCs was limited ( n = 50 exposed cases).

We found no clear evidence for an association between statin use and CC risk, with associations only observed for past use. Current research on statins and CC is limited, with conflicting results. A cohort study in the USA ( n = 2 145 593 women) reported no association [ 25 ], while a South Korean cohort study ( n = 587 705 women) found a 64% reduced CC risk among long-term users and no difference by statin type [ 20 ]. In contrast, a study in the UK Biobank ( n = 180 855 women) reported a 55% increased CC risk associated with statin use [ 28 ].

The main strength of this study is the large population, allowing evaluations in subgroups defined by statin type, and individual and cancer characteristics. However, even in this study of >1 million women, the number of cases in some subgroups (e.g. non-serous EOC histologies) was limited. The linkage with the Norwegian Prescription Database ensured no recall bias, though a limitation is the lack of data on actual use of the medications, and medications used in nursing homes was not available. An important further limitation is the lack of information on comorbid conditions associated with gynecological cancer risk. We addressed this by adjusting for medication use related to treatment of comorbid conditions. BMI is arguably the most important confounder of the association between statins and EC. BMI data were available for 42% of the study population, and BMI-adjustment did not alter the results. Another limitation was that we did not have information on the exact duration of statin use. To estimate this, we used the total number of DDDs dispensed, assuming one DDD per day. By definition DDDs are the average maintenance dose per day for a drug used for its primary indication thus DDDs are expected to be a reasonable estimate of the duration of use. We consistently observed stronger associations for past use compared to current use. Past users had shorter overall duration of use during the study period than current users, though duration of use prior to the beginning of follow-up was not quantified, and findings were similar in a sensitivity analysis where the study population excluded prevalent statin users at baseline. Given these observations, the stronger associations observed in past users may be a consequence of residual confounding or total longer-term statin use not captured during the study period.
Conclusion: Our study found that statin use is associated with a reduced risk EC, and provides no, or very little, evidence to support associations with EOC or CC. The reduced risk for EC was evident across various subgroups defined by individual (e.g. age, BMI) characteristics and tumor histology. Further studies to clarify (or confirm) associations by tumor histotype are needed for both EOC and EC.
